title: Multimodal Reranking Is a System One Decision
authors: Zhuchenyang Liu, Yao Zhang, Yu Xiao
abstract: Multimodal rerankers are usually dedicated models: a vision-language model (VLM) is trained on retrieval data to score the candidates of a query. Scoring options is not specific to reranking. System One decision models such as Jev map a state and a typed question to one probability per option without generating text, and general models can make such decisions with little or no training. Reranking is one such decision, with the query and its candidates as the state and the candidates as the options. We therefore argue that a general VLM can serve as a multimodal reranker through System One decisions, and that decision tuning can improve its reranking. We ask a VLM one choice question over the top 16 candidates of a first-stage retriever and rank the candidates by the probabilities of their labels, read from one forward pass. On MMEB-V2 image retrieval, this choice scores 5.4 to 7.3 hit@1 above a yes/no question per candidate, and the yes/no question falls below the first stage. With the choice, zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B beats the supervised Qwen3-VL-Reranker-2B on all three benchmarks and comes within 1.6 points of Reranker-8B on each. It matches Reranker-8B on MMEB-V2 visual documents (84.79 vs. 84.78 nDCG@5), at 1.1 to 1.5 times its latency. JEV-27B-VL, the same backbone tuned on text decisions only, improves page reranking by 0.6 to 1.1 points, with gains on most tasks (sign test, p <= 0.017), and leaves natural images unchanged. The zero-shot model is larger than the supervised rerankers and of a newer generation, so these comparisons are confounded; we discuss this and other alternative views, and the experiments that would test the position.
comment: Position paper. 19 pages (9 main), 2 figures, 12 tables. Code: https://github.com/Ryenhails/rerank-as-decision

title: DeclineCraft: A RAG Abstention Benchmark for Jointly Measuring Combined Retrieval and Parametric Knowledge
authors: Atharva Thakur, Abulhair Saparov, Bruno Ribeiro
abstract: Reliable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires recognizing when neither retrieved documents nor parametric knowledge supports an answer. We introduce DeclineCraft, a dynamic abstention benchmark whose unanswerable questions target Minecraft feature additions after a corpus cut-off, with audits of possible parametric exposure. Later cut-offs support evaluation of future models. Across 27 LLMs, we measure Correct Abstention Rate (CAR; how often models acknowledge insufficient knowledge on unanswerable questions), Answerable Attempt Rate and Answer Accuracy. We find that (1) single-shot retrieval significantly raises CAR in 38 of 40 configurations (model and thinking setting) versus no retrieval. (2) Iterative RAG, in which the model self-assesses its context and can request up to two further retrieval rounds, significantly lowers CAR versus single-shot RAG in 30 of 40 configurations (mean 46.4%), with little change in Answer Accuracy (68.5% to 69.3%). Adding query rewriting and reranking to hybrid (dense & sparse) retrieval lowers CAR for all 12 models tested. (3) Larger models answer more accurately (Spearman $ρ= +0.60$ with total parameters), but neither model size nor release date shows a significant association with CAR. (4) Without retrieval, enabling thinking on the same weights lowers CAR significantly for 8 of 13 models (by 14% points on average), and the responses shift from acknowledged uncertainty to premise denial.
comment: 38 pages, 28 figures, 12 tables. Code: https://github.com/Thakur-Atharva/declinecraft-benchmark

title: Robustness Analysis of Pareto-based Joint Evaluation of Fairness and Relevance in Recommender Systems
authors: Theresia Veronika Rampisela, Maria Maistro, Tuukka Ruotsalo, Christina Lioma
abstract: Recommender Systems (RSs) can be evaluated for many aspects, two of them being recommendation relevance and fairness. These two aspects can be evaluated either in isolation, using a measure for each aspect; or jointly with a single`relevance-aware' fairness measure that quantifies fairness with respect to relevance. Yet, neither approach provides a simultaneous evaluation of both relevance and fairness: the first approach may result in two different rankings of models, each corresponding to an evaluation aspect; the second approach often provides an imbalanced evaluation of the two aspects. To address this gap, we propose Distance to Pareto Frontier (DPFR), a new approach to jointly evaluate RS fairness and relevance. DPFR is based on a Pareto frontier of relevance and fairness scores from existing measures. The frontier is generated from user-item interaction data and represents various Pareto-optimal trade-offs between the two aspects. Thus, the distance from a point in the frontier provides a joint score of fairness and relevance. As DPFR can be used with existing measures, it is modular and intuitive. Our experiments with 4 recommenders and 3 fairness-aware re-rankers on 6 real-world datasets reveal inconsistent associations between existing measures and DPFR, showing that they are not reliable proxies for evaluations based on Pareto optimality. We further examine the robustness of DPFR as a joint evaluation approach for fairness and relevance by conducting experiments with artificial recommendations and with various fairness-relevance trade-offs, as well as by analysing DPFR's agreement to simple measures of fairness and relevance. These analyses show that DPFR is more robust than existing joint evaluation approaches. Finally, we provide guidelines for evaluating fairness and relevance jointly with DPFR. Our code: https://github.com/theresiavr/robustness-DPFR-recsys-evaluation.
comment: Accepted to ACM Transactions on Recommender Systems (TORS). Extension of arXiv:2502.11921(1)

title: UIBK-Embedding: Effective Text Retrieval by Unifying Dense and Late-Interaction Retrieval
authors: Abdelrahman Abdallah, Mohammed Ali, Adam Jatowt
abstract: Dense bi-encoders and late-interaction retrievers are usually treated as alternatives, yet they fail on different queries: one vector captures what a text is about, token-level matching finds its exact entities and phrases. Using both today means two models, two indexes and a score-fusion step. We present UIBK-Embedding-v1, a 179M-parameter English encoder that produces both representations in one pass and scores them with one unmodified MaxSim. The dense embedding is written into the list of token vectors as three extra vectors, and a one-dimensional tag keeps the two kinds of vectors from matching each other, so that plain MaxSim equals the token-level MaxSim plus a weighted dense cosine. The model therefore runs in a standard late-interaction index without changes; we test it with PLAID. A shared 18-layer trunk with a separate 4-layer top per head, and a cross-encoder distilled into the fused score, turn the two heads into one retriever. On BEIR, UIBK-Embedding-v1 reaches 59.79 nDCG@10. This is 2.57 points above LateOn, the strongest model of its size, and 2.10 points above it when both models read documents of the same length; UIBK-Embedding-v1 is ahead on all 15 datasets. On a decontaminated version of BEIR it stays ahead on average (61.55 against 60.36) and on 8 of 12 datasets. Among the 156 models with complete BEIR results in the MTEB results repository, only models with at least 1.5B parameters score higher. Code, model weights, and a technical blog post are available at https://github.com/DataScienceUIBK/uibk-embedding , https://huggingface.co/DataScience-UIBK/uibk-embedding-v1 , and https://huggingface.co/blog/abdoelsayed/uibk-embedding-v1 .

title: Large-Scale Biomedical RAG: Corpus Scaling, Document Representation, and Efficiency Trade-offs
authors: Adrián Sánchez-Freire, Gonzalo Pérez-Gómez, Aitziber Atutxa, Ander Barrena
abstract: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables, plus 11 pages of supplementary material. Preprint submitted to Elsevier. Code: https://github.com/hitz-zentroa/biomedical-rag-scaling and https://github.com/hitz-zentroa/qa-to-mcqa

title: Preference Is Not Position: Evaluating Reranking on NevIR in Fixed Hybrid Candidate Pools
authors: Yuning Bian, Lele Xu, Yifan Yuan, Xinyu Yin, Chengyan Zhan
abstract: Near-identical passages can differ in a decisive condition, such as negation. A ranker may order such a pair correctly while placing the preferred passage far down the retrieved list. We examine this distinction using official NevIR pairs jointly covered by fixed candidate pools from dense, learned sparse, and BM25 retrieval. On 2,736 Test query directions, a pairwise-trained ranker improves strict per-query preference over fixed fusion (56.62% versus 52.30%) while reducing preferred-passage mean reciprocal rank (MRR) from 0.5764 to 0.3055. An exploratory fixed-model replay of a variant with background sampling and revised supervision yields MRR of 0.5859 and strict preference of 54.53%. Bounded pointwise reranking of the fusion top 20 improves both outcomes. Qwen3-14B-AWQ with fusion tie-breaking reaches 77.45% strict preference, 58.99% NevIR-style paired accuracy across 1,363 complete pairs, and preferred-passage MRR of 0.7509. A BGE cross-encoder reaches 69.77% strict preference and MRR of 0.7404. A post-hoc analysis finds that the branch where equal Qwen grades for the two designated passages trigger fusion tie-breaking accounts for 27% of evaluated directions and contains most remaining strict-preference failures. These findings support joint evaluation of pairwise preference, designated-passage position, and computational cost, while distinguishing model judgments from the combined ranking procedure.
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the IEEE BigData 2026 Undergraduate and REU Consortium. Code: https://github.com/ql-link/LinkRag-Eval

title: FLMNet: Self-Ensemble Distillation from Masks to Seeds for Single-Tower CTR Prediction
authors: Yifan Wang, Yifei Du
abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction underpins recommender systems and online advertising, where high-dimensional categorical features interact in combinatorially many ways. Several recent CTR models, such as FinalNet and QNN, report higher accuracy when a network also learns from its own averaged predictions, for example by running the same network under different dropout patterns and training each run toward the average. Why this self-distillation helps, and whether its random sampling is needed, remains unclear. This work shows that as the number of dropout patterns grows without bound, the objective reduces exactly to the label loss of the logit-averaged prediction plus a penalty on how much the dropout copies of the network disagree. When dropout does not affect how a network gates its features, this penalty can be approximated in closed form, and FLMNet is designed on this principle and trains without sampling. Networks trained from different seeds disagree in the same form, and distilling several of them into one network recovers part of their ensemble gain. On five benchmarks against seventeen baselines, the resulting models take the top two places in accuracy with a single network at inference, and the gains of the penalty and of distillation, where measurable, largely add up.
comment: 44 pages, 10 figures, 15 tables. Code: https://github.com/ivanna10240823-rgb/flmnet

title: Decision4Rec: A Jev-Inspired Framework of Decision Models on Knowledge and Active Graphs for Multi-Agent Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Polignano, Het Darshan Mehta, Pasquale Lops, Ernesto William De Luca, Giovanni Semeraro
abstract: Decision models, such as the commercial Jev, are language models that return one probability for each option of a question instead of generating text. We present Decision4Rec, an open and modular framework that makes decision models useful for recommendation. A knowledge graph writes the logs of each recommendation scenario as short statements on a defined scale, such as "sold: top 10%". A pool of agents, proposes candidates, and a residual ranker keeps the best 30. A decision model, trained once on real choices of three scenarios, reads them through one interface of typed questions, and a fusion step combines its answers with the score of the ranker. Any model with this interface can be used, and we run the commercial Jev, the released open Kev and Kev models trained by us on recommendation requests. The framework with a trained 4B decision model is 25 to 36% above the best trained baseline in NDCG@10 in three sparse Amazon catalogues, one of them never used to train the decision model, and almost tie with baselines on the dense Steam dataset. Most of the gain comes from the pool, and with a trained recommender it comes from what the agents know about its candidates rather than from new candidates. The 27B decision model adds to the pool 5 to 6% above the 0.8B model in three of four domains. A trained 0.8B open model beats the released Jev in eleven of fifteen settings and is never worse. On MovieLens-1M, a dense domain never seen in training, the gain is 5 to 7%. Code, configurations and trained models are available at https://github.com/marcopoli/decision4rec and https://huggingface.co/m-polignano.

title: OpenSaC: A Python Library for Search as Code in Deep Research Agents
authors: Qi Liu, Jiaxin Mao, Fengbin Zhu, Tat-Seng Chua, Ji-Rong Wen
abstract: Deep research agents investigate complex questions through iterative search, source examination, and evidence synthesis. A conventional workflow alternates reasoning with individual search and reading actions. Search as Code introduces a new paradigm: agents write programs that compose search, source reading, reranking, model calls, and local processing, returning selected observations for further reasoning. To support this workflow in existing coding agents, we present OpenSaC, an open-source Python library with a companion Search as Code skill. Configurable capability interfaces let agents combine these operations while retaining evidence for inspection and reuse. Compared with standard Codex using its built-in web search, the OpenSaC configuration uses less execution time and fewer model tokens on BrowseComp and WideSearch, with higher accuracy on BrowseComp and slightly lower row F1 on WideSearch. We aim to lower the barrier to adopting Search as Code and provide an open foundation for community development and transparent research on deep research agents.
comment: Source code: https://github.com/liuqi6777/OpenSaC

title: Cross-Pollination Retrieval: Finding Transferable Ideas Across Fields in Scientific Literature
authors: Seokwon Jung, Yerang Kim, Yejin Kim, Alexander Rubinstein, Arnas Uselis, Sangwoo Park, Seong Joon Oh, Sangdoo Yun
abstract: Many scientific advances come from cross-pollination, carrying an idea from one field over to a problem in another. Yet retrieving papers across fields remains underexplored, with existing benchmarks confined to a narrow range of fields. We study cross-pollination retrieval, the problem of identifying transferable ideas across research fields, and introduce CPR-Dataset, a large-scale dataset constructed by mining cross-topic citations. Its evaluation split CPR-eval has 1,300 queries in 26 fields, and its training split CPR-train has 10,573 pairs. On CPR-eval, the best of eleven existing retrievers reaches a Recall@10 of only 0.26, whereas an LLM reranker reaches 0.81. Standard contrastive fine-tuning on CPR-train raises Recall@10 to as high as 0.70. The gain carries over to domains held out from training and to analogy and reasoning-intensive retrieval. On AnaloBench, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 33% over the untrained retriever, whereas training on three existing retrieval datasets lowers it. On BRIGHT, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 70%, more than twice the gain from those datasets. CPR-Dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/CPR-Dataset, and the code at https://github.com/SeokwonJung-Jay/Cross-Pollination-Retrieval.
comment: 35 pages, 11 figures, 19 tables

title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
authors: Luigi Rivolta
abstract: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. Code is public; models and data will be released.
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Code: https://github.com/luiginotmario/hum2song

title: MEMORA: A Memory-Enhanced Multimodal Committee Reranking Agent for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval
authors: Mohamed Mahmoud, Mostafa Farouk Senussi, Mahmoud Abdalla, Mahmoud SalahEldin Kasem, Abdelrahman Abdallah, Hyun Soo Kang
abstract: Reasoning-intensive retrieval is fundamentally challenged when queries demand deep semantic inference and arrive in multimodal form. Existing systems treat each query in isolation, rely on monolithic rerankers, and lack retrievers trained for cross-modal reasoning. We introduce MEMORA, a Memory-Enhanced Multimodal Orchestrated Reranking Agent built around three contributions: (1) Collaborative Factor-Committee Reranking, which decomposes queries into intent factors, extracts factor-specific evidence into a structured matrix, and synthesizes judgments via a memory-conditioned meta-verdict model; (2) an Episodic Memory Module that tracks factor outcomes across queries and dynamically adjusts priorities at inference time; and (3) a Reasoning-Aware Dense Retriever fine-tuned with chain-of-thought augmentation on 20k+ reasoning-intensive pairs. Evaluated on MM-BRIGHT across 29 domains, MEMORA achieves nDCG@10 of 41.5 (text-to-text) and 38.9 (multimodal query-to-text), outperforming the strongest agentic text-only baseline by +8.3 points and the strongest agentic multimodal baseline by +7.9 points. Code and data are available at https://github.com/HarnessLab/MEMORA.
comment: Accepted at EMNLP Main 2026

title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering
authors: Debopriyo Banerjee, Owais Aijaz, Ahmer Tabassum, Zhuohan Xie, Preslav Nakov, Veselin Stoyanov
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks- MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP, a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues, and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K-1M characters. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG.

title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
authors: Jeonghwan Choi, Jibin Hwang, Hayoon Park, Hyeonjae Cheon, Hwanjun Song
abstract: Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi-source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross-source orchestration rather than scaling alone. Code and data are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/DISL-Lab/RetailBridge}.
comment: Preprint. Under review

title: Structure-Aligned History Learning with Subspace-Structured Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
authors: Kaiwen Wei, Kejun He, Jie Zhang, Xiaomian Kang, Yuming Yang, Aijia Zhou, Xie Zhou, Yining Wang, Nayu Liu, Li Jin, Zhenyang Li, Jiang Zhong, He Bai, Jingxuan Wei, Junnan Zhu
abstract: Generative recommendation constructs semantic IDs for catalog items and predicts the next ID from user interaction histories. However, existing methods face limitations in both stages. First, conventional quantizers may produce imbalanced code assignments and lack coherent intermediate semantic units between individual tokens and complete items, limiting history reconstruction. Second, recommendation models remain dominated by next-item prediction, treating historical interactions mainly as conditioning context and providing limited supervision for recovering persistent preferences across the historical path, particularly when relevant preference signals are distributed over distant interactions. To address these limitations, Structure-Aligned History Learning (SAHL) reconnects the two stages by using the structure created during quantization directly for history reconstruction. Its Semantic Residual Balanced Quantization (SRBQ) forms a balanced token-subspace-item hierarchy, and SAHL reconstructs history at these same granularities. Predictive entropy prioritizes uncertain transitions, while curriculum optimization progressively shifts training to inference-aligned next-item prediction. On four Amazon Review categories, SAHL improves NDCG@10 by 18.6%-30.0% over RPG and 2.7%-6.0% over strong method MHL. Controlled analyses verify balanced code use, the benefit of following quantizer-defined groups during reconstruction, and dependence on user history. The relevant code is available at https://github.com/CQU-MM-Intelligent-Lab/SAHL.
comment: 34 pages, 10 figures, including references and appendices

title: RAGit: Turning Document Preprocessing into an Experimental Variable for RAG
authors: Omar El Bachyr, Saad Ezzini, Tegawendé F. Bissyandé, Jacques Klein
abstract: Document preprocessing choices can substantially affect retrieval in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, yet they are often selected heuristically and are difficult to compare under consistent conditions. We present RAGit, an open-source experimentation workbench for the systematic and reproducible evaluation of document preprocessing choices through downstream retrieval. RAGit represents parsing, chunking, indexing, retrieval, and evaluation as configurable experimental stages, enabling controlled comparisons while the remaining downstream settings are kept fixed. It preserves provenance from retrieved chunks to source pages and maps heterogeneous retrieval units to a common page-level ranking for evaluation. The current implementation supports multiple parsers and chunking strategies, dense and late-interaction retrieval, reusable intermediate artifacts, and multi-configuration benchmarking. We demonstrate RAGit through controlled experiments comparing alternative preprocessing configurations under a fixed retrieval setup, illustrating how preprocessing can be treated as an explicit experimental variable. RAGit and its documentation are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/OmarElbachyr/ragit). A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/tsst-Bhfz4I.
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at the Tool Demonstration Track of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Software Engineering Conference (APSEC 2026)

title: Optimal Fusion Weights Form Intervals, Not Points: A Latency-Aware Study of Query-Adaptive WRRF
authors: Iris Ma, Zahra Shekarchi, Stuart Mcilroy, Mahtab Farrokh, Fattane Zarrinkalam, Joel Stremmel
abstract: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is widely used to combine sparse and dense retrievers in hybrid information retrieval, but a critical limitation is that it assigns a fixed, uniform weight to each retriever regardless of the query. Query-aware methods treat the per-query optimal weight as a single point, an assumption whose empirical validity has not been examined. We present an empirical study of eight dynamic fusion weight prediction strategies across four datasets and four sparse--dense retriever pairs. When we compare these approaches to static fusion and a per-query oracle that bounds achievable performance, several findings emerge. First, the per-query optimal fusion weight is typically an interval rather than a point. Queries can have multiple optimal intervals, and these can take on a variety of shapes. Second, 74 of 128 dynamic fusion methods tested were significantly better than standard RRF after false discovery rate correction. Third, dynamic fusion methods exhibit differing quality and latency characteristics that should be considered when choosing an appropriate fusion method. To address this last finding, we present a tiered decision framework that maps practitioner constraints, dataset properties, label availability, hardware, and latency budget to an appropriate method class. We release the code for our experiments at https://github.com/thomsonreuters/query-based-rrf.

title: Code Skill Server: A Large-Scale Search Engine for Code Generation Skills
authors: Xiaoyong Li, Haolong Li, Dongliang Xu, Haoyu Li, Yifan Wang, Jingyuan Shi, Yanghua Wang, Yanbin Sun, Shidong Pan, Yue Yao
abstract: Agent skills have proven to be an effective technique for improving agent ability on specific tasks, including software engineering, natural science, and mathematics. During such a process, using agent skills often involves manually discovering and organizing skills from heterogeneous sources, while existing skill retrieval methods mainly focus on selecting relevant skills from established skill libraries. However, with the rapidly increasing number and variety of reusable agent skills, manually searching for relevant skills across heterogeneous sources is becoming impractical at scale. In this paper, we introduce the Code Skill Server (CSS), a large-scale search engine for finding the most useful code generation skills for a target task. CSS consists of a skill server that incrementally collects and indexes publicly available code generation skills from multiple sources, with 993 skills included in the corpus used in this work. Extensive experiments across different retrieval methods and code generation benchmarks show that the best CSS configuration improves Pass@1 by up to 13.91% and consistently improves all evaluated models by at least 4.21% in the cross-model evaluation. These results demonstrate that CSS can effectively search for and serve relevant skills, improving code generation quality and enhancing models' code generation capabilities. Code and the CSS-993 corpus are available at {https://github.com/haoyuli-sdu/CodeSkillServer}.

title: Reasoning Reranking with Semantic IDs as the Sole Item Representation
authors: Zhenwei Tang, Jintao Liu, Di Bai, Xidong Wu, Xinwu Cheng
abstract: Reasoning rerankers write a rationale before ranking a candidate slate, and existing systems read item metadata to do so, even though generative recommenders increasingly represent items as compact Semantic IDs (SIDs). Ranking from SIDs alone has two appeals: SID prompts are far shorter than the matched item text, and although item codes are fixed from content, the backbone learns their token embeddings in part from user-item interaction sequences, so the tokens can carry behavioral signal that item text lacks. That training targets next-item generation, and whether it supports ranking a supplied slate from SIDs alone is untested. We build ReRankID, a controlled testbed in which models reason and rank from a history and slate shown only as SIDs, varying item rendering, history length, and slate size one at a time. On this testbed, such models often copy the input order instead of reranking, and readable metadata does not repair the failure. We compare supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled self-training, on-policy distillation, and verifier-based reinforcement learning as post-training methods and find that they elicit the missing behavior. The strongest post-trained model, the 8B model trained with a graded ranking reward, gives the best SID-only ranking and matches strong text-reading LLMs whose prompts are about 20x longer. It ranks above random with no history at all, where a caption-reading reference does not, and it keeps its gains at long histories, where text prompts pass 50k tokens and the caption-reading reference stops improving. In a paired rationale audit, this model argues trade-offs better than that reference but describes items less accurately. The common post-training methods we test thus elicit ranking from SIDs but not faithful item descriptions, which calls for post-training that improves the reasoning itself, not only the ranking it produces.
comment: 30 pages, 3 figures. Code: https://github.com/lilv98/ReRankID ; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/lilvjosephtang/ReRankID

title: Improving OCR Accuracy Through Multi-Classifier Verification of Visually Similar Characters
authors: Nuzhat Khan, Ab Al-Hadi Ab Rahman, Mohamad Anuar Kamaruddin, Muhammad Paend Bakht, Sana Fatima, Farhad Khodadadi, Ibrahim Yousef Alshareef
abstract: Distinguishing visually similar characters is a persistent challenge for optical character recognition (OCR) systems, causing errors in critical applications of text digitization. While preprocessing techniques improve image quality and word-level post-processing corrects spelling errors, neither addresses character-level visual ambiguity, an intrinsic property of certain character pairs that limits even state-of-the-art OCR models. We present the Character Verification Model (CVM), a character-level post-processing framework that verifies and corrects ambiguous characters in OCR outputs using specialized binary classifiers trained on visually confusable pairs such as 'O'/'0', 'Z'/'2', and 'S'/'5'. CVM operates independently of dictionary validation, making it suitable for non-lexical data including serial numbers, alphanumeric codes, and license plates. Experiments on three OCR engines (Tesseract, EasyOCR, TrOCR) and ten fonts with low to high complexity demonstrate accuracy improvements of 3.95-14.81 percentage points, with an 87.3% correction rate for visually similar character errors and a false-correction rate of only 2.3%. The modular architecture integrates with existing OCR pipelines without modification to underlying recognition models.
comment: 32 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to Computer Vision and Image Understanding (CVIU). Dataset available at https://github.com/VeCAD-P04-UTM/94-Class-ASCII-Image-OCR-Data

title: AuditKIT: A Unified Evaluation Spine for Benchmarking, Judging, and Comparing Large Language Models and Agentic Systems
authors: Shreeyans Arora, Utsav Avaiya, Zera Lyngkhoi, Hem Gosalia, Ram Mohan Rao Kadiyala, Vinay Kumar Sankarapu, Pratinav Seth
abstract: Evaluating language models and agents requires combining benchmark accuracy, judge-based assessment, runtime performance, tool-use behavior, and retrieval quality. Differences in interfaces, metric semantics, and trace formats complicate these comparisons and can hide failures in agentic workflows. We present AuditKIT, a source-available evaluation library that records these measurements in one result representation, with direction-aware metric contracts, configuration fingerprints, and extensible metrics and backends. For agents, it provides turn-aware tool-call matching, separates parallel from sequential execution, and distinguishes verified task outcomes from trajectory-level diagnostics. Missing or unobservable evidence is marked unscored rather than counted as failure. For retrieval-augmented generation, it combines ranked retrieval metrics, judged grounding, and deterministic evidence checks. Seven case studies spanning model comparison, serving runtimes, retrieval, tool calling, and interoperability show how answer extraction, runtime behavior, and metric selection change evaluation outcomes.
comment: 25 pages, 2 figures, 13 tables. Code: https://github.com/Lexsi-Labs/AuditKIT. Shreeyans Arora and Utsav Avaiya contributed equally; work done while at Lexsi Labs

title: Star Light, Star Bright: Can Multimodal Models Parse an Astronomy Visual Question Answering Dataset Right?
authors: J. P. Naiman
abstract: Figures are essential for scientific communication, and the field of Visual Question Answering (VQA) aims to test the figure understanding capabilities of large multimodal models (LMMs). Here, we investigate the accuracy of several low-cost LMMs on domain-specific VQA tasks for astronomical images of the sky. As instrument for this task we build a domain-specific VQA dataset comprising 2001 partially-synthetic figures divided evenly between contour plots, real telescope images drawn from NASA's SkyView, and "fake" sky images which share the axes and angular scales of the real images but draw their colors from a gaussian mixture model, alongside 47357 questions. Each figure is released as pristine and with realistic page-aging degradations mimicking the historical astronomical corpus. Testing three low-cost proprietary LMMs, we find models frequently fail to answer domain-specific questions at high accuracy. An initial comparison with 104 human-verified, astrometrically tagged figures from historical journal publications shows similar median errors in angular extent. All code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/jnaiman/SkyImagesWASP2026 and dataset is available on HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/astro_sky_image_vqa.
comment: 5 main pages, 12 pages total, accepted to The 4th Annual Workshop for Artificial Intelligence for Scientific Publications (WASP) 2026, International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing & Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (IJCNLP-AACL)

title: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression Ability across Large Language Models
authors: Weiting Liu, Zhiyu Pan, Shuhong Wang, Zhenquan Yao, Jungang Li, Li Zhao, Jian Jiang, Jianfeng Feng, Ai Han, Wenlian Lu
abstract: Context compression in long-running applications of large language models (LLMs) must preserve goal-relevant information, often before specific downstream questions are known. We introduce GACC-Bench, a benchmark for Goal-Adaptive Context Compression that evaluates how reliably LLMs adapt information retention to specified high-level goals. For each source context, we derive one or more high-level goals by grouping source-grounded questions according to shared downstream objectives. The benchmark contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 document and agent-trace contexts from seven collections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. The compressor receives a source context, a goal, and a context-length budget, with the associated evaluation questions withheld. A fixed reader answers these questions individually using the same compressed context. Our evaluation of ten LLM compressors reveals substantial gaps to full-context performance even for the best-performing model, particularly in supporting correct answers to every question associated with a goal. Compared with goal-agnostic compression, target-goal conditioning consistently improves accuracy, whereas mismatched-goal conditioning reduces it. GACC-Bench is available at https://github.com/weiting24/GACC-Bench.

title: Retrieved but Not Read: Understanding Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail to Use Available Evidence
authors: Owen Walters, Lihu Chen, Francesca Toni
abstract: Web search allows LLMs to access up-to-date information, but it remains unclear why they sometimes produce outdated answers even when relevant evidence is available. To study this problem, we construct temporal facts whose values changed after the models' training cutoffs. We evaluate one proprietary model under deployed web search and six open-weight model configurations under controlled retrieval. We find that models often answer from search snippets without opening the source pages, which is associated with higher rates of outdated answers and unfaithful citations. Our controlled experiments and layer-wise analysis reveal a gap between the availability of evidence and its effective use. Even when retrieved evidence influences internal predictions, models may still favour outdated information in their final answers. We hope these findings will help advance research on the reliable use of retrieved evidence in search-augmented LLMs.
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 16 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/ojwwalters/retrieved-but-not-read

title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
authors: Zidong Jia, Guofu Xie, Xiao Zhang
abstract: Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output-level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165--228x faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.
comment: Accepted at CIKM 2026

title: ReviewPilot: A Multi-Agent System for Screening and Data Extraction in Systematic Reviews
authors: Zhaoqian Xue, Shaoze Zhou, Xuexin Li, Junting Mu, Haozheng Liu, Zhongyin Wang, Yichun He, Renkai Ma, Hao Zhou, Sarah Bratt, Siyuan Ma, Chen Chen, Lingyao Li
abstract: Systematic literature reviews follow the PRISMA process of screening scholarly works and extracting evidence from included studies. Deep research tools based on large language models (LLMs) can search and summarize the literature but do not record which studies are excluded or where extracted values come from. We develop a conversational multi-agent system called ReviewPilot that automates the PRISMA workflow from paper screening to information extraction. Researchers can tailor criteria and schemas through dialogue, and a project memory keeps their configurations and revisions. Each screening decision comes with its reason and each extracted value with its source. On epidemiological expert reviews, ReviewPilot outperforms a single-prompt LLM and AgentSLR across three LLMs, with screening macro F1 up to 0.776 and extraction F1 up to 0.788. Case studies in biomedicine and human-computer interaction show close agreement with human annotators, suggesting that ReviewPilot can transfer beyond epidemiology. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhaoqianXue/ReviewPilot.

title: HCFM: Helmholtz Component Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Shyam Sundar Saravanan, Tie Luo, Sanjay Madria
abstract: Flow Matching (FM) is an efficient simulation-free approach for training flow-based generative models, making it a promising foundation for scalable time-series anomaly detection (TSAD). However, standard FM learns a monolithic vector field in which nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled. This creates a central challenge for TSAD; local expansion and contraction carry crucial anomaly-sensitive information, yet isolating this signal requires expensive Jacobian-trace estimation over the entire field. We propose \emph{Helmholtz Component Flow Matching} (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the vector field prediction network with separate transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head is constrained to be divergence-free, so divergence estimation is restricted to the compression head, while a lightweight residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch. This structured parameterization improves scalability and detection performance by separating volume-preserving nominal transport from density-changing compression, yielding cleaner anomaly signals from distinct deviations of nominal behavior. Experiments on large-scale univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks show that HCFM consistently improves detection accuracy while maintaining efficient inference compared with 16 baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustAIoT/HCFM__time-series-anomaly/
comment: To appear as a conference paper in ICDE 2027

title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
authors: Milind Srivastava, Zeying Zhu, Peilin Xin, Yancheng Yuan, Zaoxing Liu, Vyas Sekar
abstract:
Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app-level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost-latency tradeoffs at scale. Ideally, system operators would like immediately deployable and backwards compatible solutions to improve the cost-latency tradeoffs without significant impact on the fidelity of their observability applications. Unfortunately, existing solutions including state-of-art timeseries databases and custom approximate querying solutions fail on one or more aspects.
  In this paper, we present the design and implementation of TurboProm, a backwards-compatible drop-in accelerator for metrics observability deployments. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic-preserving summary view rather than classical query-centric view. Instead of estimating query results on raw timeseries metrics data, TurboProm uses semantic-preserving summaries that enable high-fidelity analytics with significant cost-latency improvements. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state-of-art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. TurboProm is open-source at https://github.com/ProjectASAP/ASAPQuery.

title: Same Query, Different Answer: Run-to-Run Variance in Semantic Query Processing
authors: Oktie Hassanzadeh, Dharmashankar Subramanian
abstract: Semantic query engines ask a large language model (LLM) to judge individual rows, and benchmarks compare these engines on the quality of a few executions at temperature 0. We measure how much another execution changes. We re-execute the text and tabular workloads of SemBench, LRO-Bench, and UDA-Bench through their own harnesses, log every one of 1.2 million model calls, and reanalyze SemBench's published executions. At temperature 0, between 0.07% and 10.2% of rows change their operator output over five executions, depending on the model, and up to 24.0% on one task. Plans amplify these changes exponentially in the number of rows an answer exposes, as a possible-worlds model predicts: on UDA-Bench, a few percent of extracted values change, but about two thirds of the answers do. In SemBench's published results, 21% of text results change quality between executions, including on engines whose plans are deterministic. Several per-query system comparisons, and 16 of 28 tests of LRO-Bench's implementation recommendations, are not settled by the executions the benchmarks run. Changing rows are rows on which models disagree with each other; identical requests within one execution disagree as often as across executions; and one execution's decision margin or reasoning length predicts which rows change. Voting reduces the variance but does not remove it, and a calibrated cascade keeps its guarantee while the rows it returns change. We derive reporting rules for benchmarks and design rules for engines.
comment: Code and data: https://github.com/semviews/sqp-variance-study

title: Time-Varying Favorite-Longshot Bias in Polymarket Weather Markets
authors: Shouchen Qiu, Huaijun Qiu
abstract: Prediction-market prices combine traders' judgments about future outcomes, but their errors may be concentrated in particular price ranges and change as settlement approaches. Prior cross-category evidence shows that Polymarket weather markets have larger pricing bias than other major categories, without separating low-price longshots from high-price favorites. This study compares the two ranges at different horizons in daily maximum-temperature markets. Event-level probability scores, cubic B-spline recalibration, and Buy-NO tests are used to examine the form and effect of the bias. Longshot overpricing mainly occurs at distant horizons, whereas favorite overpricing becomes much stronger during the final 1-12 hours and is nearly one order of magnitude larger. Event-level scores improve toward the daily temperature peak, while simple recalibration yields no statistically significant gains. The Buy-NO results in the corresponding time windows also show that the main pricing error is concentrated at the favorite end.
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the IEEE ICDM 2026 Teen Research Symposium (Teen Track), Shenyang, China, November 2026. Code available at https://github.com/ShouchenQiu/PolyWeatherData

title: CALQA: Conformal Screening of Forecast-Ensemble Configurations from One Mergeable State
authors: Xiufeng Liu, Ruyu Liu, Yusen Liu, Huan Huo, Per Sieverts Nielsen
abstract: AutoML systems fit ensemble weights over model libraries; a search can score, per category, market or time pane, thousands of weightings of the quantile-averaged (Vincentized) ensemble for the narrowest conformally calibrated interval; exact calibration scores a group's rows per candidate. We present CALQA, a fixed-size integer aggregate per group and pane that stores histograms of normalised block scores at a net of weight vectors. One GROUP BY builds it; it merges by addition, retracts deletions by subtraction and scores any candidate without reading a row. We prove that its score never falls below the exact split-conformal shift and exceeds it by at most the net distance plus a grid gap; that coverage carries over to each fixed weight vector and, for i.i.d. blocks and up to a union-bound slack, to a searched weight vector deployed with the state's shift; and how small any such state can be. The state is thus a screen: it ranks all candidates, and exact recomputation re-checks the top 100. On five public panels (604 groups, 10,000 candidates each) this two-stage plan matches exact search on held-out blocks (99.95% of its Winkler score), 1.3-59 times faster. On two real panels of about $10^8$ rows (smart meters, retail sales) it is 44-54 times faster at 99.98-100.01% of that score and beats sample screens with the same re-check in regret at less total time. Picks deployed with their exact shift need a held-out coverage check. The state does not pay off for small or greedy searches, off-net weights at ample memory or full twelve-member support.
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Extended version with full proofs. Code: https://github.com/xiufengliu/calqa

title: Semantic Views: Certified Reuse of LLM Labels Across Semantic Queries
authors: Oktie Hassanzadeh, Dharmashankar Subramanian
abstract: Semantic query engines evaluate natural-language filters with a large language model, and every evaluation is a costly oracle call. Optimizers that reduce these calls face a dilemma: cascades that trust a cheap proxy miss their precision and recall targets on many queries, methods with finite-sample guarantees save little, and all of them discard the oracle's labels when the query ends. We present SemViews, a certified semantic filter that orders tuples by signals that cost no oracle calls (the labels that earlier queries left behind as semantic views, a local embedding, and a helper model's score), refines that order with labels it must pay for anyway, and certifies its answer with fresh stratified oracle samples. The answer meets user precision and recall targets with probability at least $1-δ$ for every workload and every catalog, so a stale or misleading view can cost oracle calls but never accuracy. On four workloads replayed against 725,000 recorded oracle labels, SemViews meets both targets on 99.63% of queries and saves 28%-45% of the oracle calls, whereas the only prior method in our study with the same guarantee needs 1.32x-1.71x as many calls. When a question returns in different words, views cut its calls by a further 27%-36%, with both targets met on at least 99.8% of such queries; similarity caches and entailment-based reuse meet them on only 17%-47%.
comment: Code and data: https://github.com/semviews/lotus-semviews

title: Soft Voting for Policy-Aware Private Data Synthesis
authors: Yingge Hu, Gautham Ramesh Babu, Mostafa Milani
abstract: Blowfish privacy relaxes differential privacy (DP) by protecting only the attribute-value substitutions a data owner specifies as edges of a policy graph. A sparser policy can reduce the noise required by a mechanism, but only when the released statistic changes less across protected substitutions than across arbitrary DP neighbors. We study this question for evolutionary, nearest-neighbor DP synthesizers such as Private Evolution (PE) and its tabular instantiation Tab-PE, which score private records against a candidate population and release a noisy vote histogram. Their hard vote is constant inside each candidate's decision region and jumps at its boundary. Its policy-specific sensitivity therefore equals the full worst-case value whenever at least one protected substitution crosses a boundary, regardless of how short that substitution is. Because every round we examined contained such a substitution, the policy graph gave no reduction in noise. We propose BF-Soft, a temperature-smoothed soft vote whose response changes gradually with distance. Its sensitivity has a tight closed-form bound in the policy graph's reach and the temperature, independent of the number of candidates, and the bound can be computed once before synthesis. It also predicts from the policy alone when policy-aware smoothing cannot substantially reduce noise: protecting a flat categorical or binary attribute drives the reach to its maximum. On real and synthetic datasets under narrow numeric policies, BF-Soft reduces error relative to hard voting at strong privacy budgets, while the advantage reverses at weaker budgets. A public-data pilot predicts when soft voting is beneficial without spending private budget.
comment: 22 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables. Extended version with full proofs and additional experiments. Code: https://github.com/ayanamirei629/Soft-Voting-for-Policy-Aware-Private-Data-Synthesis

title: LDPGraph: Locally Differentially Private Graph Synthesis by Exploiting Neighborhood Structure
authors: Jiawei Dong, Zhikun Zhang, Quan Yuan, Zhe Liu, Yunjun Gao
abstract: The widespread application of graph data inevitably brings significant privacy risks, as its unprotected use can lead to the leakage of sensitive information. These risks are particularly acute in the setting with an untrusted curator, where the data remains decentralized and each user only holds the connections to their neighbors. To mitigate such privacy risks, we adopt local differential privacy (LDP) to collect users' private information and generate a synthetic graph. However, existing methods suffer from either excessive noise injection by perturbing the local adjacency lists or significant structural information loss due to the simplistic graph encoding process. To address these issues, we propose LDPGraph, an effective graph synthesis algorithm that takes one step further by exploiting neighborhood structures under LDP. To obtain neighborhood statistics beyond degrees, LDPGraph aggregates a noisy global view from perturbed adjacency lists and combines it with projected local connections to estimate node-level triangle counts. To correct the structural inconsistency caused by separately perturbing degree and triangle count, LDPGraph jointly refines them into feasible degree-triangle targets. To reconstruct a global graph from these estimated targets, LDPGraph adopts a triangle-first strategy that first preserves local clustering structures and then fulfills remaining degree requirements. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets and multiple commonly used graph metrics validate the superiority of LDPGraph. Source code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-TrustAID/LDPGraph.
comment: Accepted at IEEE ICDE 2027. Extended version with appendices

title: Correspondences as Decisions: JevNexus for Decision-Centric Schema Matching
authors: Runze Li, Hanchen Wang, Ying Zhang, Wenjie Zhang
abstract: Schema matching increasingly uses generative language models to rerank retrieved column candidates, although the underlying task is a bounded correspondence decision. We present JevNexus, which combines typed pairwise decisions with schema/instance evidence and invokes listwise refinement only when the evidence disagrees and the fused margin is small. The evaluation covers 561 cases from six benchmark families. JevNexus obtains dataset-macro MRR and Hits@1 of 0.930 and 0.909, compared with 0.926 and 0.903 for Magneto, while reducing mean latency from 123.452 to 15.929 seconds (7.750). Paired analysis finds no statistically significant difference in either MRR or Hits@1. The gate invokes listwise refinement for only 5.665% of source columns and avoids the degradation caused by unconditional refinement. Code and experimental artifacts are available at https://github.com/RazeenLI/JevNexus.
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures

title: Building Navigable Graphs Without Search in Three Composable Stages
authors: Édgar Chávez
abstract: Navigable graphs can be built without searching for neighbors: partition the data, evaluate every pair inside each part, and select each point's edges from the candidates. We give such a construction in three separable stages and show that the middle one decides the quality. The pool is any partition with a few memberships per point. The ending turns a point's candidates into out-edges; ours keeps a bounded heap, prunes by occlusion with a per-corpus slack, and appends reverse edges, re-pruning only where a list overflows. The spine is any edge set, exempt from the prune, that keeps the graph reachable from its entry; ours, half-space-proximal edges over a random sample, routes monotonically to every sampled point and replaces a spanning tree at 1/10 to 1/500 of its cost. The ending composes with any partitioner: on PiPNN's own candidate pool it beats PiPNN's ending on each of six corpora from $10^6$ to $10^8$ points, by 3 to 14% in distance evaluations at equal recall, and with 60 to 120 memberships per point the composed build matches or beats a full dense construction at k=10 and k=100 on all six, in 0.5 to 0.9 of its build time, deterministically. The analysis explains why. Once a pool is localised its quality is set by the data: every pool built on GIST lands within 4% of the exact-kNN ceiling, and the pairs a block cover misses are predicted, point by point, by the local clustering of the kNN graph, whose zero-clustering tail sets the memberships a corpus needs and grows with n. All code, patches and logs are public.
comment: 26 pages. Code: github.com/zevahcle/graft-ann (branch fgraft); experiments, logs and patches: github.com/zevahcle/fgraft-experiments
